input.question: Why do we define the point of no return from a black hole (Schwartzchild radius) with a speed, instead of total energy required?
input.ground_truth: In general relativity, the curvature of spacetime sort of flips when you cross the horizon. Space becomes timelike and time becomes spacelike. A consequence of this is that the only paths through spacetime are towards the center. Moving away from it is equivalent to going back in time. This is independent of the fact that the escape velocity on the surface is light speed.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why do we define the point of no return from a black hole (Schwartzchild radius) with a speed, instead of total energy required?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, strong bathtub with a drain that pulls things in super fast (that’s like a black hole). There’s a special line around the drain called the “point of no return.” If you get closer to the drain than that line, you can’t swim out anymore, even if you try your hardest. 

Now, scientists use “speed” to tell you if you’re too close, because it’s easier to see how fast you’re moving toward the drain. If you’re going too fast, or too close, you can’t escape. 

They don’t use “total energy” because it’s trickier to explain and measure for every single thing. It’s much simpler to just check: “Are you past this line?” and “How fast are you going?” That way, you know if you can get out or not!
